title: Cebularz, Pierogi with Bryndza and Roztocze Trout
lead: The cuisine of the Lublin region is a mix of Polish, Ukrainian, and Jewish traditions. Find out what is worth eating in a region where East and West meet. Slow travel through Lublin cuisine.
body:
Why Lublin cuisine, differently

The cuisine of the Lublin region is borderland cuisine — Polish, Ukrainian, and Jewish influences meet here. This is visible in the dishes: pierogi with bryndza, cebularze, krupnik, groats, potatoes. All simple, earthy, and deeply filling dishes. The Lublin region is in southeastern Poland, on the border with Ukraine, where Poles, Ukrainians, Jews, and Armenians lived side by side for centuries — and each of these cultures brought something to the local cuisine.

Slow travel through Lublin cuisine is a celebration of taste and tradition. Instead of rushing from restaurant to restaurant, stop in one longer — in a village inn, in a milk bar, in an agritourism farm. Each dish has its own story, its own cook, its own village. Ask where the ingredients come from, how the dish is prepared, who passed down the recipe. This is a journey that rewards those who slow down — the longer you are in one place, the more flavors you can truly get to know.

What to see

Lublin cuisine splits into several categories: flour dishes (cebularz, pierogi with bryndza, pierogi with groats), potato dishes (pancakes, babka, kiszka), meat dishes (duck with apples, game), fish dishes (Roztocze trout, carp), baked goods (kołocz, cheesecake, makowiec), liqueurs (śliwowica, herbal liqueurs). Exploring the culinary region of the Lublin region takes 2–3 days.

Flour dishes

  • Lublin cebularz — one of the most recognizable dishes of the region. Flat yeast dough with onion and poppy seeds, sold at markets and bakeries throughout the Lublin region. Inscribed on the EU protected products list. Worth trying for breakfast, with fresh butter.
  • Pierogi with bryndza — delicate pierogi with sheep cheese, a specialty of the Polish-Ukrainian borderland. Served with cracklings or sour cream.
  • Pierogi with buckwheat groats — a regional variant, popular in the Lublin region. Served with cracklings or onion.
  • Pierogi with cabbage and mushrooms — a traditional Lenten dish, served at Christmas Eve. In the Lublin version — with marjoram and pepper.

Potato and meat dishes

  • Potato babka — a baked dish of grated potatoes, bacon, onion, and eggs. Served with sour cream or mushroom sauce. A classic of eastern Polish cuisine.
  • Potato sausage (kiszka ziemniaczana) — sausage made of potato mass with bacon, baked in the oven. Served with onion and mustard.
  • Potato pancakes — in the Lublin version with marjoram and bacon. Served with sour cream or mushroom sauce.
  • Duck with apples — roast duck with apples and marjoram, a Lublin classic. Available in elegant restaurants.
  • Boar in mushroom sauce — roast or stewed boar with mushroom sauce. Served with dumplings or potatoes.

Fish and baked goods

  • Roztocze trout — fresh, grilled or from the grate, with horseradish and lemon. One of the best dishes you can eat in the region.
  • Lublin carp — carp from local farms, prepared in various ways: fried, baked, in jelly. Served at holidays and family celebrations.
  • Lublin kołocz — sweet yeast cake with streusel and various additions. Baked for weddings and family celebrations.
  • Lublin cheesecake — cheesecake with curd cheese, raisins, and orange peel. Available at pastry shops in Lublin.
  • Lublin makowiec — yeast cake with poppy seeds, dried fruit, and icing. Served at holidays and family celebrations.
  • Śliwowica — a local plum liqueur, available in shops with local products.

When to go

  • April–June — the best time for slow travel. Fewer tourists, fresh seasonal produce, long days. Worth a walk through markets.
  • July–September — season for fresh vegetables, fruit, mushrooms. Worth it for markets and culinary festivals.
  • September–October — season for mushrooms, pumpkins, plums. September and October are good times for mushroom picking in the forests of the Lublin region.
  • November–March — season for bigos, krupnik, duck. Worth it for winter cuisine, especially during the holiday season.

Getting there

Lublin cuisine is from the eastern region of Poland — best to travel by car or train, connecting several towns in one trip.

  • By train: Lublin, Zamość, Chełm have railway stations, with connections from most Polish cities.
  • By car: ~2.5 hours from Warsaw (S17), ~3.5 hours from Kraków (DK79 and DK19), ~2.5 hours from Rzeszów (DK19).
  • By bus: PKS and private operators serve most towns on the route.

How much time you need

A weekend (2 days) is the minimum — Lublin (milk bars, cebularz, pierogi with bryndza) and surroundings.

Three days is realistic for a first visit. Lublin, Zamość, Kazimierz Dolny, Roztocze.

A week lets you explore the whole culinary region of the Lublin region — all the most important dishes and places.

What to eat and where to sleep

Instead of restaurants, choose milk bars and village inns. There, cooks prepare what they have known since childhood, and they do it best.

  • Lublin cebularz — a Lublin classic, available at bakeries in Lublin.
  • Pierogi with bryndza — a borderland classic, available at milk bars in Lublin.
  • Roztocze trout — fresh, grilled, available at local smokehouses in Zwierzyniec.
  • Duck with apples — a Lublin classic, available in elegant restaurants.
  • Lublin makowiec — sweet cake, available at pastry shops in Lublin.
  • Beer from local breweries — several craft breweries in the region (Browar Zakładowy, Browar Perła).

Accommodation: Lublin (largest choice, more options), Zamość (town, more options), Kazimierz Dolny (small town, more options), Zwierzyniec (small town, smaller choice), agritourism farms in villages (quiet, home-cooked food).

Practical tips

  • Milk bars — usually open from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m., often closed on weekends. Check hours before your trip.
  • Regional restaurants — look for places where cooks prepare traditional recipes. Avoid tourist restaurants in city centres.
  • Culinary workshops — many farms and agritourism businesses offer workshops (baking cebularze, making pierogi, baking bread). Book ahead.
  • Diet — Lublin cuisine can be heavy and filling. Eat smaller portions to try more dishes.
  • Markets — the best place to buy local products (cheeses, honey, cold cuts, mushrooms).
  • Weather — weather in the region can be changeable. Even in July, bring a rain jacket.
  • Signal — good in towns, weaker in villages. Have an offline map.
tip: Order cebularz at one of the bakeries in Lublin — preferably fresh, with fresh butter, for breakfast. It is the most authentic version of this dish.
